title: The Cyrillic alphabet: new shapes
objectives: I can read the thirteen new letters 'б', 'г', 'ґ', 'д', 'ж', 'з', 'л', 'п', 'ф', 'ц', 'ч', 'ш' and 'щ' in capital and small form, and say their names.
I can tell 'г', a voiced 'h', from 'ґ', the 'g' of 'go', and read 'дж' and 'дз' as single sounds.
I can keep a voiced consonant voiced at the end of a word, as in 'хліб'.
I can recognize the handwritten and italic shapes of 'т', 'и', 'п' and 'д'.
I can ask 'Що це?' and 'Хто це?' and answer with 'Це' and a noun.

vocabulary.note: With family words Ukrainian usually leaves out 'my' when it is clear whose relative is meant, where English adds it.

example.source: Who is there? My brother.

vocabulary.note: The animal and the food.

example.source: What is this? This is fish.

vocabulary.note: The 'г' is [ɦ], a voiced 'h' (note 2).

example.source: This is the head, and this is the nose.

vocabulary.note: The 'ґ' is [g], the 'g' of 'go' (note 2). Other forms use the stem 'ґанк-', without the second vowel.

example.source: This is the porch.

vocabulary.note: Two of this unit's sounds in one word: 'ґ' [g] and 'дз', one sound [d͡z]. Said [ˈgud͡zɪk].

example.source: What is this? A button.

vocabulary.note: The building and the idea of home. Other forms use the stem 'дом-', with 'о' in place of 'і'; a later unit explains this change.

example.source: Here is a house, and there is a school.

vocabulary.note: The 'ж' is [ʒ], the 's' of 'measure'. The word also means 'wife'.

example.source: There is a woman over there.

vocabulary.note: The 'з' is [z], as in 'zoo'.

example.source: It is winter here.

vocabulary.note: Other forms use the stem 'стол-', with 'о' in place of 'і', the same change as in 'дім'.

example.source: This is a table, and this is a window.

vocabulary.note: The final 'б' stays a voiced [b], as in English 'rib' (note 4).

example.source: The bread and cheese are here.

vocabulary.note: Both the place and the letters and parcels it handles.

example.source: The post office is there.

vocabulary.note: A borrowed word that never changes its form, while most Ukrainian nouns change their endings, as later units show. The 'ф' is [f].

example.source: This is a café.

vocabulary.note: The 'ц' is [t͡s], the 'ts' of 'cats'. Other forms use the stem 'цукр-', without the second vowel.

example.source: What is this? Sugar?

vocabulary.note: The 'ч' is [t͡ʃ], the 'ch' of 'church'. Other forms use the stem 'вечор-', with 'о' in place of 'і'.

example.source: It is evening here.

vocabulary.note: The 'ш' is [ʃ], the 'sh' of 'shoe'. The word names a school for children, not a university.

example.source: The school is here.

vocabulary.note: The soup made with beets that the culture note describes. The final 'щ' is [ʃt͡ʃ]: [bɔrʃt͡ʃ].

example.source: The borscht is here, and the bread is there.

vocabulary.note: Asks about a thing. The 'щ' makes it [ʃt͡ʃɔ], one syllable.

example.source: What is over there?

vocabulary.note: Said [bd͡ʒɔˈlɑ]: 'б' and then the single sound 'дж'. Ukrainian asks 'хто', 'who', about a bee, as about any animal (note 6).

example.source: What is that? It is a bee.

vocabulary.note: The 'дз' is one sound, [d͡z], as in 'adze'. It names any small bell: a doorbell, a bicycle bell, the school bell.

example.source: What is this? It is a doorbell.

vocabulary.note: Points at a thing or a person, near or far, and never changes its form (note 6). It sounds like the name of the letter 'ц'.

example.source: What is this? It is juice.

dialogues.title: At the market
dialogues.context: Sam is at a covered market in Kyiv. He points at the things on Bohdan's stall and asks what they are. At the next stall, Bohdan's mother sells coffee and borscht.

lines.source: And over there? What is over there?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.source: Bread and sugar are over there.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.source: No, the coffee is over there.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: And who is that over there?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Це ма́ма. Там борщ і ка́ва.

dialogues.title: Pictures in class
dialogues.context: In class, Iryna Petrivna holds up pictures and Sam names what he sees. 'Петрі́вна' is her patronymic, a name made from her father's first name, which the culture note explains.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна

dialogues.title: A parcel at the post office
dialogues.context: Olena has hurt her hand, so her brother Taras fills in the sender's lines of a parcel form for her at the post office. She spells her name and her street, Khreshchatyk, letter by letter.

lines.speaker: Оле́на

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: О, ел, е, ен, а. А тут?

lines.speaker: Оле́на

grammar.title: Thirteen new letters
grammar.explanation:
Unit 1 taught the fourteen letters whose shapes look like English letters. This unit teaches thirteen more, all consonant letters, with shapes that English does not use. Together the two units cover 27 of the 33 letters of the alphabet, and unit 3 adds the last six. The principle has not changed: each letter stands for one sound, or for a small set of sounds chosen by a rule you can see in the word. Of the letters taught so far, only 'щ' always stands for two sounds together.

Most of the new sounds exist in English, so the main work is learning the shapes. Some shapes are easy to remember by what they resemble:

- 'б' looks like the digit 6.
- 'з' looks like the digit 3.
- 'ч' looks like the digit 4.
- 'г' looks like an 'L' flipped top to bottom.
- 'ґ' is 'г' with a small hook on top.
- 'щ' is 'ш' with a small tail.
- 'п' looks like a gate: two posts and a bar.

Three sounds need care. 'г' is not the 'g' of 'go'; note 2 explains it. 'щ' is two sounds written with one letter, [ʃ] followed by [t͡ʃ], like the 'sh ch' of 'fresh cheese' said without a break. 'л' is a darker 'l', like the 'l' of 'full', with the back of the tongue raised; before 'і' it is lighter, like the 'l' of 'leaf', because a consonant before 'і' is said with the tongue raised toward the palate, as unit 1 showed.

Two smaller points make the sounds more exact. Like 'т', the letters 'д', 'з', 'ц' and 'л' are said with the tip of the tongue touching the back of the upper front teeth. Like 'т' and 'к', the letter 'п' has no puff of air after it, as in English 'spin' rather than 'pin'.

The letter names follow three patterns:

- The consonant followed by 'е': 'бе', 'ге', 'ґе', 'де', 'же', 'зе', 'пе', 'це', 'че'.
- 'е' followed by the consonant: 'ел', 'еф', like 'ем' and 'ен' from unit 1.
- The consonant followed by 'а': 'ша', 'ща', like 'ка' and 'ха'.

The name of 'ц' is 'це', which sounds the same as the word 'це' that note 6 teaches. In the table, Letter gives the capital and the small form, Sound gives the symbol in square brackets, and English gives the nearest English sound. A small arc joining two symbols, as in [t͡ʃ], marks them as one sound. A small raised stroke before a syllable, as in [ˈgud͡zɪk], marks that syllable as stressed, as the stress mark over a vowel does in Ukrainian words.

grammar.title: 'г' and 'ґ'
grammar.explanation:
'г' and 'ґ' are two letters for two different sounds, and the spelling tells you which sound to say.

'г' stands for [ɦ], a voiced 'h'. English 'h' is breath only. Voice is the buzz of the vocal cords that you feel when you put your fingers on your throat and say 'zzz'. Ukrainian 'г' is an 'h' with that buzz added. The 'h' in the middle of English 'ahead' comes close, because many speakers voice it between two vowels: say 'ahead' slowly, keep the buzz going through the 'h', and then say 'голова́' starting with the same sound.

'ґ' stands for [g], the 'g' of 'go'. It is a rare letter, found in a small number of Ukrainian words and in some names and words from other languages. Ukrainian words with 'ґ' include:

- 'ґа́нок', porch
- 'ґу́дзик', button
- 'ґрунт', soil
- 'ґа́ва', crow

No rule predicts which words have [g], so learn the 'ґ' together with each word that has it.

Many words borrowed from other languages are written with 'г' where English has a 'g', and they are said with [ɦ]: 'газе́та', newspaper, and 'гара́ж', garage. Read what is written, not what the English word suggests.

The rule has one exception. Before 'к' or 'т', 'г' loses its voice and is said [x], the 'ch' of Scottish 'loch': 'ле́гко', easily, is said [ˈlɛxkɔ]. Note 4 explains voice in consonants.

grammar.title: 'дж' and 'дз': two letters, one sound
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian writes two of its sounds with two letters each: 'дж' is [d͡ʒ], the 'j' of 'jam', and 'дз' is [d͡z], the 'dz' of 'adze' or the 'ds' of 'beds'. Inside a root they are one sound, said in one movement of the tongue, not a 'д' followed by a separate 'ж' or 'з'. The root is the part of a word that carries its basic meaning, the way 'kind' is the root of 'unkind' and 'kindness'.

Because each pair is one sound, it can stand wherever a single consonant can: at the start of a word, after another consonant or between vowels.

- 'джерело́', spring of water, begins with [d͡ʒ].
- 'бджола́' has [b] and then the single sound [d͡ʒ].
- 'дзво́ник' begins with [d͡z].
- 'ґу́дзик' has [d͡z] in the middle: [ˈgud͡zɪk].

The rule stops at the edge of a root. A prefix is a piece added before a root to change its meaning, like 'un-' in 'unkind'. When a prefix ends in 'д' and the root begins with 'з' or 'ж', the two letters are two sounds. In 'відзна́ка', award, 'від-' is a prefix and the root is the one in 'знак', sign, so you say [d] and then [z]. Such words are few, and this course points them out when they appear.

grammar.title: Voiced consonants stay voiced
grammar.explanation:
A voiced consonant is said with the vocal cords vibrating, and a voiceless consonant is said without them. Put your fingers on your throat and say 'zzz' and then 'sss': you feel a buzz in the first and none in the second. The tongue is in the same place for both; only the voice differs. Ukrainian sorts its consonants into eight such pairs, shown in the table. In seven of them the two sounds are made in the same place. 'г' [ɦ] is made in the throat and 'х' [x] between the back of the tongue and the roof of the mouth, but 'г' is the closest voiced sound to 'х', and Ukrainian treats the two as a pair.

The rule: Ukrainian keeps a voiced consonant voiced at the end of a word and before most other consonants. So the spelling shows the sound:

- 'хліб' ends in [b], as English 'rib' does.
- 'ніж', knife, ends in [ʒ].
- 'ка́зка', fairy tale, has [z] before [k].
- 'ло́жка', spoon, has [ʒ] before [k].

Two words can differ in nothing but the voice of their last consonant: 'плід', fruit, ends in [d], and 'пліт', raft, ends in [t]. Say the last consonant of a word fully, with the voice continuing to its very end, and do not let it fade into its voiceless partner.

Where the rule stops: 'г' before 'к' or 'т' is said [x], as note 2 shows with 'ле́гко'. Later units explain a few other changes between neighboring consonants, each where it first appears.

grammar.title: Handwritten and italic letters
grammar.explanation:
Italic is the slanted style of print used for emphasis, and handwriting joins letters into a flowing script. In both, a few small letters take shapes that look like different English letters. You will see them on café menus, shop signs, notes and the board in class, so learn to recognize them. This course never asks you to write by hand.

The four small letters that mislead English readers most:

- 'т' looks like an English 'm', so 'тут' can look like 'mym'.
- 'и' looks like an English 'u', so 'сир' can look like 'cup'.
- 'п' looks like an English 'n'.
- 'д' in handwriting often looks like an English 'g'.

Only the shape changes. Each one is the same letter with the same sound, and capital letters keep shapes close to their printed forms. When a handwritten word looks like an English word that makes no sense, read it again with these four shapes in mind.

grammar.title: 'Це', 'що' and 'хто': pointing and asking
grammar.explanation:
A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun, as 'it' and 'who' do in English. 'Це' is a demonstrative pronoun, a pointing word: you use it to point at a thing or a person, near or far. English needs 'this', 'that' or 'it' together with 'is' for this job. Ukrainian uses 'це' alone, and 'це' never changes its form.

'Це хліб.' means 'This is bread.' Word for word it is 'this bread': Ukrainian has no word here for 'is', as unit 1 showed with 'Ма́ма тут.', and it has no words for 'a' and 'the', so the same sentence also translates 'That is the bread.' Unit 5 explains both facts.

To ask what something is, put a question word before 'це':

- 'Що це?' asks about a thing.
- 'Хто це?' asks about a person or an animal.

Ukrainian asks 'хто' about people and animals alike. A teacher pointing at a picture of a cat or a bee asks 'Хто це?', literally 'who this?', where English says 'What is this?'. The answer starts with 'Це': 'Це кіт.', 'Це Оле́на.'

A question without a question word uses the same words as the statement, with the voice rising at the end: 'Це сир?' means 'Is this cheese?'. The answer is 'Так' or 'Ні'. To point at one more thing, start with 'а', 'and': 'А це?' means 'And this?'.

As unit 1 showed, the vocabulary labels each noun masculine, feminine or neuter, and the ending usually shows the group: 'брат' and 'хліб' are masculine, 'ри́ба' and 'шко́ла' feminine, 'вікно́' and 'мі́сто' neuter. 'Кафе́' is neuter for another reason: a borrowed noun that names a thing and never changes its form is usually neuter. Unit 5 explains what gender does.

Most Ukrainian nouns change their ending to show their job in a sentence, as unit 5 explains. The part of a noun that comes before the ending is its stem. In some nouns the stem itself changes in those other forms, as 'кіт' becomes 'кота́' in unit 1, and the vocabulary notes give the changed stem so that you will recognize the word later:

- 'дім', house, has the stem 'дом-'.
- 'стіл', table, has the stem 'стол-'.
- 'цу́кор', sugar, has the stem 'цукр-', without its second vowel.

examples.source: Who is this? This is Olena.
What is that? It is a cat.

culture.title: The letter 'ґ', patronymics and borscht
culture.text:
The letter 'ґ' has a history of its own. Ukrainian writers used it from the seventeenth century to write the rare sound [g]. In 1933 the Soviet authorities removed it from the official Ukrainian spelling, and for more than fifty years words such as 'ґа́нок' and 'ґу́дзик' were printed with 'г', although many speakers went on saying [g]. The letter returned in 1990, in a revised edition of the official spelling rules, and the current rules of 2019 keep it.

A Ukrainian's full name has three parts: a first name, a patronymic and a family name. A patronymic is a name made from the father's first name. A woman's patronymic usually ends in '-івна' and a man's in '-ович': the daughter of a man named 'Петро́' has the patronymic 'Петрі́вна', and his son has 'Петро́вич'. So 'Іри́на Петрі́вна' is Iryna, daughter of Petro. Students address a teacher, and adults address an older person they do not know well, by first name and patronymic together, which is the respectful form. The 'в' of 'Петрі́вна' comes before a consonant, so it is said [w], as in 'cow', as unit 1 taught.

'Борщ', the soup Bohdan's mother sells in the first dialogue, is made with beets and is one of the best-known Ukrainian dishes. Every region, and nearly every family, has its own recipe. In 2022 UNESCO added the culture of cooking Ukrainian borscht to its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.

exercises.prompt: What sound does 'г' stand for at the start of 'голова́'?
exercises.explanation: 'г' is an 'h' said with voice, as at the start of 'голова́'. The [g] of 'go' is written 'ґ'.
'ґ' is 'г' with a small hook on top, and it stands for [g], as in 'ґа́нок'.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter name with its letter
How is 'щ' said, as at the end of 'борщ'?
exercises.explanation: 'щ' is two sounds written with one letter, [ʃ] and then [t͡ʃ], said without a break.
The name of 'ц' is 'це', which sounds the same as the pointing word 'це'. The name of 'ч' is 'че'.
'Сир' ends in 'р'. 'Сік', juice, ends in 'к', and 'ри́ба', fish, has two syllables.
'Ґа́нок' begins with [g]. 'Ґу́дзик', button, and 'дзво́ник', bell, both have the sound [d͡z].

exercises.hint_source: What is this? This is bread.
exercises.explanation: 'Що' asks about a thing. Its 'щ' makes it sound [ʃt͡ʃɔ].

exercises.hint_source: Who is this? This is Oksana.
exercises.explanation: 'Хто' asks about a person or an animal.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English

exercises.explanation: 'Цу́кор' begins with [t͡s], and 'там' means 'there'. 'Тут' would mean 'here'.
'Дж' is one sound, [d͡ʒ], so the word begins [bd͡ʒ].

exercises.hint_source: What is this? It is a button.
exercises.explanation: The word has 'ґ' for [g] and 'дз' for the single sound [d͡z].
Ukrainian keeps a voiced consonant voiced at the end of a word, so the 'б' stays [b].

exercises.hint_source: Spelling the word 'хліб' aloud, letter by letter.
exercises.explanation: The name of 'б' is 'бе': the consonant followed by 'е'.

exercises.prompt: How many sounds does 'дж' stand for in 'бджола́'?
exercises.explanation: Inside a root, 'дж' is one sound, said in one movement of the tongue.

exercises.prompt: Written by hand or in italic, the word 'тут' can look like which English letters?
exercises.explanation: Small 'т' looks like an English 'm' in italic and in handwriting, and 'у' looks like 'y'.
'Дзво́ник' begins with [d͡z]. 'Ґу́дзик' begins with [g], and 'бджола́' with [bd͡ʒ].

exercises.prompt: Iryna Petrivna points at a picture of a cat. Which question does she ask?
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian asks 'хто' about people and animals alike.

exercises.hint_source: The school is here, and the café is there.
exercises.explanation: 'Там' means 'there', and 'тут' means 'here'. The word 'а' joins the two contrasting statements.

exercises.prompt_source: Who is there? It is Olena.
What is over there? It is a café.
What is this? Is it fish?
exercises.explanation: Ask with 'Що це?'. A question without a question word keeps the words of the statement and raises the voice at the end.

exercises.prompt: 'Плід' means 'fruit' and 'пліт' means 'raft'. What tells the two words apart when they are spoken?
choices: The last consonant: voiced [d] against voiceless [t]
exercises.explanation: A voiced consonant stays voiced at the end of a word, so 'плід' ends in [d] and 'пліт' in [t].

exercises.prompt_source: The fish is here, and the cheese is there.

exercises.explanation: 'Це' points, and there is no word for 'is' or 'a'. 'Д' is [d], as in 'dog'.

exercises.prompt_target: Ха, ер, е, ___, а, те, и, ка.
exercises.hint_source: Spelling the street name 'Хреща́тик' aloud, letter by letter.
exercises.explanation: The fourth letter is 'щ', named 'ща'. 'Ша' is the name of 'ш', which has no [t͡ʃ] after the [ʃ].

exercises.prompt_source: Spell the word 'борщ' aloud, letter by letter.

exercises.explanation: 'Борщ' ends in 'щ', and 'хліб' ends in a voiced 'б'.
'По́шта' has 'п', 'ш' and 'т'. Both word orders are correct.

exercises.prompt: In 'відзна́ка', 'award', the letters 'д' and 'з' are two sounds, not one. Why?
choices: 'від-' is a prefix, so 'д' ends one part of the word and 'з' begins the root.
exercises.explanation: 'Дз' is one sound only inside a root, as in 'дзво́ник'.

exercises.hint_source: The bread is here, and the sugar is there.
exercises.explanation: 'Хліб' ends in 'б', and 'цу́кор' begins with 'ц'.
'І' joins the two nouns. Ukrainian needs no word for 'is'.

exercises.prompt: Which word is said with [x] although it is written with 'г'?
exercises.explanation: Before 'к' or 'т', 'г' loses its voice and is said [x]: [ˈlɛxkɔ]. Everywhere else 'г' is [ɦ].

exercises.hint_source: This is a school, and over there is the post office.
exercises.explanation: 'Шко́ла' has 'ш', and 'по́шта' has 'ш' followed by 'т'.
